Selectivity is another key issue to be addressed in order to achieve practical application. For PFAS sensors, selectivity should be compared not only with other organic or inorganic interferents in water but also within the PFAS family itself, and this requires a more subtle design for PFAS-capturing probes based on a deeper understanding of the PFAS −probe interactions. Meanwhile, considering the abundance of PFAS members and the requirement for e ﬃ cient detection, a sensor that enables multiple-analyte detection at the same time is essential. This need also calls for better probe design as well as eﬃ cient data processing techniques. As the development of novel PFAS sensors progresses, standards for evaluating and comparing sensor performance will become increasingly important. Sensitivity, selectivity, and reliability are the most basic and crucial parameters of PFAS sensors. For the sensitivity or limit of detection of the sensor, guidelines provided by o ﬃ cial agencies (e.g., USEPA) could be used as standard criteria, which are typically below 70 ng/L. retrieved_context.text: Electrochemical oxidation is generally employed downstream of concentration technologies such as IXR or foam fractionation rather than being applied directly to PFAS- impacted groundwater. This treatment sequence reflects several key constraints at environmentally relevant concen- trations. First, PFAS levels in groundwater typically span the ng L −1 to μg L −1 range, where mass transfer limitations restrict removal efficiency at the electrode surface. Second, the direct application of electrochemical oxidation to groundwater would require prohibitively large electrode areas and high energy input given the large water volumes involved, whereas treatment of concentrated residual streams enables more efficient operation. Third, because PFAS degradation by electrochemical oxidation follows approximately first-order kinetics, higher influent concentrations (mg L −1 ) are associated with reduced specific energy demand compared to μg L −1 influent levels. Finally, the increased solution conductivity of concentrated waste streams alleviates ionic limitations and enhances the effective active area of the reactor, thereby improving overall treatment performance. Key performance metrics for electrochemical oxidation of PFOA include E EO per log removal of PFOA, PFOA removal, and y F . Conclusions and recommendations The degradation of PFAS represents a major challenge for several sectors (academic, public health, industrial and regulatory, among others). It is evident that significant efforts have been made to develop different technologies capab le of degrading these substances. Several studies agreed on the advantages of the application of AOP for the degradation of PFAS. However, most of these oxidation systems have only been tested at laboratory scale, and full -scale industrial and practical ap plications have rarely been carried out, high cost being one of the main reasons for the lack of scalability of the processes. Larger and more rigorous studies are crucial to produce scientific evidence on the efficiency of AOP in PFAS degradation. Similar to sensor research, the selectivity of sorbents is crucial but hard to compare as it is greatly impacted by the experimental conditions. Furthermore, few papers of PFAS sorbents demonstrated and discussed the selectivity by comparing the adsorption performance between PFAS and its interferents individually; instead, most of them examined the selectivity as the anti-interferent ability by showing an una ﬀected PFAS adsorption performance in the presence of interferents. This method is not unreasonable in terms of demonstrating the selectivity, but at the same time, one should pay attention to the dosage of sorbents, the species of selected interferents, and the concentrations of all analytes in sample solutions and make sure the una ﬀected performance is not caused by overloading of sorbents or using unrealistic sample solutions. Since the adsorption performance is largely related to the initial concentration of PFAS analyte, all sorbents should be tested under environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations (ng/L to μg/L). However, most existing research conducted adsorption experiments in batch mode under unrealistic initial concentrations (>mg/L), 36,115 which cannot truly re ﬂect the capability of those sorbents in real applications. Direct decomposition is desirable in that ideally it does not create an additional waste stream; rather, the compound is disassembled chemically to harm- less by-products. Key questions regarding PFAS treatment include what is the fate of the shorter chains produced, and is the advanced method also appropriate to treat these shorter chains? Such ques- tions have not been settled to date. 8 In this work, plasma treatment is applied to the treatment of PFAS-contaminated ground water. While plasma treatment is often thought of as an advanced oxidation method, it has been shown that oxidation is not effective in decomposing short chain PFAS compounds. 8 This is largely due the relative strength of the C –F bond and the high electronegativity of fluorine. The oxidation potential of fluorine is larger than that of OH, the chief radical in advanced oxidation. The literature search was conducted using Web of Science and Google Scholar, focusing on studies related to PFAS removal using biochar. The search keywords included PFAS, removal, biochar, water matrix, adsorption, emerging contaminants, activated biochar, removal mecha- nisms, biochar characterization, biochar regeneration, and water treatment technologies. This study focuses on the following key aspects: (1) efficiencies of removal of PFAS using biochar, modified biochar, biochar composites, and biochar-incorporated hybrid treatment; (2) elucidation of PFAS removal mechanisms when using biochar; (3) bio - char and PFAS physico-chemical properties influencing removal mechanisms; (4) influence of water matrix proper- ties including pH, Natural Organic Matter (NOM) and ion contents, and temperature on PFAS removal efficiency; (5) assessment of reusability of biochar for treating PFAS-con- taminated water; and (6) challenges in scalability and eco - nomic feasibility of using biochar. Hence, this review article attempts to answer the following scientific questions: (1) What are the mechanisms of removal of PFAS when using biochars originating from different sources? (2) What are the physico-chemical properties of biochar and PFAS that may influence the removal of PFAS from water?

Currently, computational simulation studies on the decomposition of PFAS mainly use quantum mechanics methods [48 – 51] . While it is established that SCWO environments can effectively degrade fluorinated compounds, there is a notable lack of research on the reaction mecha - nisms of PFAS under these conditions. This gap hinders the optimization of SCWO reactors for treating aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) and PFAS-contaminated waste [41] . To address this, this study selected perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) as a representative compound and employed the ReaxFF reactive force field to simulate its pyrolysis and supercritical water oxidation at the atomic level. The pyrolysis simula - tion aims to uncover the formation mechanisms of the primary in - termediates and final products of PFNA under anaerobic conditions. In contrast, the SCWO simulation focuses on elucidating its oxidation pathways and product evolution under high temperature, high pressure, and oxygen conditions. The integration of these two approaches not only enables a systematic analysis of the multi-stage reaction mechanisms of PFNA in typical disposal environments but also provides a theoretical foundation for optimizing SCWO reactor parameters. 2.

Supercritical Water Oxidation SCWO leverages the supercritical phase of water that is achieved by increasing the temperature and pressure of a water- based liquid to a minimum of 374 °C and 218 atm, respectively, as demonstrated in Figure  2. Supercritical water has a relatively high density compared to water vapor at ambient conditions (approximately one- third of the den - sity of liquid water at atmospheric conditions). In this phase, oxygen is fully soluble, resulting in rapid and complete oxi- dation of organics and transforming the feedstock into car - bon dioxide (CO2), water, and inorganic salts, as shown in Figure  3. When SCWO is applied to PFAS, organic fluorine is mineralized to inorganic fluoride. A major advantage of SCWO over other PFAS destruction technologies is its abil- ity to destroy lower molecular weight, shorter chain PFAS compounds (6 carbon chain structures, or C6, and below) in addition to higher molecular weight, legacy PFAS com - pounds (8 carbon chain structures, or C8, and above). The rapid reaction time, on the order of 2 to 10 s, allows for con- tinuous processing and potential for scale- up while mini - mizing the equipment footprint required (Max et al. 2022).

In this study, the C/H/O/ F ReaxFF force field developed is used to simulate the reaction behavior of PFNA under pyrolysis and SCWO conditions. The initial decomposition pathway, main intermediates, and product formation mechanisms were elucidated. Two classes of PFAS, perfluoroalkyl car - boxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), are commonly found in legacy stockpiles, in - dustrial waste streams, and as environmental pollutants. Continuous flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) reactors have been shown to destroy several PFAS and aqueous film-forming foams. However, a direct com - parison of the SCWO efficacy for PFSAs and PFCAs has not been reported. We show the effectiveness of continuous flow SCWO treatment for a matrix of model PFCAs and PFSAs as a function of operating temperature. PFSAs appear to be significantly more recalcitrant than PFCAs in the SCWO environment. The SCWO treatment results in a destruction and removal efficiency of 99.999% at a T > 610 ◦ C and at a residence time of ~30 s. Fluoride recovery lags destruction PFAS at 510 ◦ C and reaches > 100% above 610 ◦ C, confirming the formation of liquid and gaseous phase intermediate product during lower temperature oxidation. Supercritical water treatment Above its critical point (T c = 374 ◦ C, P c = 22.1 MPa), water becomes a non-polar solvent, which can efficiently dissolve organic substances and gases [36] . The ion product constant of supercritical water (SCW) is over five orders of magnitude lower than that of water at ambient conditions, facilitating free radical reaction pathways [37] which have been utilized in gasification [38 – 40] , partial oxidation [41] , and SCWO [42 – 44] processes. SCWO process benefits from the high free radical environment to convert organic compounds via oxidative reaction mechanisms into CO 2 and H 2 O, with the hydroxyl radical (OH*) being the primary oxidizing species [45 – 49] . Heteroatoms are converted to corresponding inorganic acids or salts, such as HCl, HF, sulfates, phosphates, etc. High-density homogeneous SCWO environment facilitates fast and more complete oxidative reactions. Water as the reaction medium allows for simulta - neous oxidation and hydrolysis mechanisms [50] , enabling the more complete destruction of some recalcitrant wastes.

Introduction Water above 374°C and 22.1 MPa becomes supercritical, a special phase of water with both liquid-like and gas-like properties. Above the critical point of water, most organic compounds are soluble, oxygen is fully miscible, and salts are insoluble ( Hodes et al. 2004 ; V oisin et al. 2017). In the presence of an oxidizing agent, such as oxygen, supercritical water ’s unique properties accelerate the oxidation of a broad range of organic pollutants. Since the 1980s, supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) has been used successfully to treat a variety of hazardous wastes, such as chemical warfare agents and halogenated compounds ( Abeln et al. 2001 ; Cohen et al. 1998 ; Kim et al. 2010 ). Technical challenges have limited implementation of SCWO at scale, including the buildup of corro- sive species during the oxidation reaction and salts’ precipitation on the reactor body, leading to high maintenance and operation costs (Marrone 2013; Mitton et al. 2001 ). This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. Second, adsorption is simple in both the syn- thesis of adsorbents and their use. Contact time and adsorption kinetics Adsorption kinetics influence the practicality of PFAS removal, especially in flow-through systems. Traditional adsorbents such as PAC often require extended contact times (up to several hours) to reach equilibrium (Son and An 2022). By contrast, nano-engineered adsorbents and hybrid materials, due to their high surface-to-volume ratios and reactive interfaces, tend to exhibit rapid uptake, often reaching equilibrium within min - utes (Birch et al. 2022). Rapid adsorption kinetics are essential for developing efficient point-of-use treatment technologies and scaling up continuous treatment systems. Pr esenc e of na tur al or ganic ma t ter (NOM) NOM, including humic and fulvic acids, can adversely affect PFAS adsorption by competing for active sites or altering adsorbent surface properties. NOM may introduce steric hindrance, reduce porosity through fouling or shift surface charges, thereby diminishing PFAS removal efficiency (Qi et al. 2022). Strategies such as pre-filtration, adsorbent surface modification or the development of anti-fouling materials can help mitigate these effects and improve per - formance in natural water matrices. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. The removal of PFAS by GAC can be explained by several mecha - nisms, including hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic attraction, and PFAS aggregation ( Du et al., 2014 ). PFAS compounds vary significantly in hydrophobicity: carbon chain length is proportional to hydropho - bicity, and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) demonstrate increased hydrophobicity as compared to perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) with the same perfluorinated carbon chain length ( Park et al., 2020 ). As such, GAC treatment has been found to be more effective for removing longer-chain PFAS than shorter-chain ones, and more effective for removing PFSA than PFCA ( McCleaf et al., 2017; Westreich et al., 2018 ). Traditional full-scale GAC treatment facility design is typically based on empty bed contact time (EBCT) and media service-life, often described by the number of bed volumes (BVs) the system can treat until solute breakthrough ( Crittenden et al., 1987 ).
